verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, on the Gittith, of the sons of Korah, a mizmor.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung upon the Gittith, a psalm of the sons of Korah.
verses.directors_commentary: A heading, not a verse to act: it tells the musicians what to do. 'Choirmaster' (לַמְנַצֵּחַ) is from a root meaning 'to lead' or 'to excel', so he is the one who conducts the Temple singers; the KJV's 'chief Musician' is fair. The Gittith is a mystery. Ancient readers took it as an instrument or tune 'of Gath', or as a vintage song tied to the winepress (גַּת); nobody knows, and the safest course is to leave the word as it stands. The Korahites were a family of Levitical singers and gatekeepers (the Chronicler places them at the Temple thresholds), which quietly prepares verse 11, where the speaker would rather linger at a threshold than live in comfort elsewhere. The KJV puts the heading outside the numbered verses (84:0) and shifts every later verse down by one; the Hebrew counts it as verse 1.

philological_notes.note: Meaning unknown: an instrument or melody from Gath, or a song for the winepress (gat). Left untranslated.
'Of/for the sons of Korah': the preposition לְ can mean authorship, dedication or guild. The Korahite singers appear in a cluster of psalms (42–49, 84–85, 87–88).

verses.translation_literal: How beloved [are] your dwellings, YHWH of hosts!
verses.translation_dramatic: How lovely they are, your dwelling places, LORD of hosts. How dear.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a cry, not a statement. 'How…!' (מַה) breaks out before the speaker has finished arranging a sentence, so play it as an exclamation, a breath, and only then the name. The KJV's 'amiable' has drifted: in 1611 it meant 'lovable', but a modern audience hears 'friendly', which is far too tame. The word is יְדִידוֹת, from the root of 'beloved' (the same root as David's name and as 'Jedidiah'); these are places one loves as one loves a person. 'Dwellings' is a plural (מִשְׁכְּנוֹת) and the KJV's 'tabernacles' sounds like a tent of cloth; the Hebrew is simply 'places where someone lives', the whole sanctuary complex as God's home. The title 'YHWH of hosts' (the commander of armies, heavenly and earthly) sits in tension with the tender word: the king of armies is loved at his front door.

philological_notes.note: 'Beloved, lovely'. Related to dod 'beloved' and to the name Yedidyah. It describes things that are dear, not merely pleasant.
Plural of mishkan, 'dwelling place'. The plural may be intensive, or may point to the courts and rooms of the sanctuary.

verses.translation_literal: It has longed, and also it has been consumed, my soul, for the courts of YHWH; my heart and my flesh, they sing out to the living God.
verses.translation_dramatic: My whole self aches for the courts of the LORD. It longs; it is worn thin with longing. My heart, my very flesh, cry out in joy to the living God.
verses.directors_commentary: Two verbs, both about desire, the second stronger than the first: נִכְסְפָה is 'to pine', כָּלְתָה is 'to come to an end, to be used up'. The speaker is not merely homesick but wasting. Ibn Ezra reads the 'and also' as marking just this overshoot of ordinary longing, and Rashi compares כלה with David's longing after Absalom (2 Sam 13:39). The KJV's 'fainteth' captures the exhaustion; 'courts' is accurate, and the courts were the open spaces where the people gathered, not the shrine itself (Radak). The subject 'my soul' is the נֶפֶשׁ, the throat and appetite of the living person, not a ghost inside; 'heart and flesh' complete the picture, the inner and outer person together. The KJV 'crieth out' hides that the verb is רנן, a ringing shout of joy; it is a happy noise, not a wail, and a second tension with the exhaustion of the first half. 'The living God' is a polemic phrase, set against idols and the dead gods of neighbouring peoples. The verb 'they sing out' is plural, though 'heart' and 'flesh' are two separate things; the Hebrew lets them speak together.

philological_notes.note: 'To long, to pine' (cf. Gen 31:30, the root of 'silver' only by coincidence of spelling). Describes strong desire.
'To come to an end, to be spent'. Here: the soul is used up by longing, a step beyond 'longed'. Compare Psalm 119:81.
'To ring out, to shout for joy'. Not a lament. The piel is intensive.

verses.translation_literal: Even a bird has found a house, and a swallow a nest for herself, where she has set her young, [at] your altars, YHWH of hosts, my king and my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the sparrow has found a house, and the swallow a nest for herself, a place to lay her young, here, beside your altars, LORD of hosts, my King and my God.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker looks at the smallest creatures in the sanctuary and is jealous. The sparrow (צִפּוֹר, a general word for a small bird) and the swallow (דְּרוֹר, a name that also means 'freedom') have what he lacks: a settled place beside God's altar. The KJV's 'sparrow' and 'swallow' are reasonable guesses; Ibn Ezra says only that the bird is known in Spain and Radak names a small bird by a French word, so neither is certain. Drama: the Hebrew sentence runs breathlessly on, with the main point, 'your altars', held back until the end, as if the speaker cannot quite say it. The KJV smooths a feature: the preposition אֶת-, 'with, beside', is turned to 'even', which makes the altars an apposition to the nest; the Hebrew simply says the young are placed with the altars. Whether the scene is a standing Temple or a ruined one is disputed: Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the Temple in ruins where birds nest; Radak notes that in the working Temple birds were kept off the roof (the 'raven-scarer'), so the verse most naturally means a ruin or a high place. Pitch the line in either case as bitterness and longing: the bird has found a home; I have not. A reader steeped in the ancient world would also hear the ordinary fact that altars stood in the open and that birds nested near any shrine; the claim here is the contrast with the speaker. The final two phrases, 'my king' and 'my God', turn a speech about birds into a personal confession.

philological_notes.note: A bird, usually 'swallow'. The same word means 'freedom, release' (Lev 25:10), and Ibn Ezra offers that it is so called because the bird sings only when free.
'Her fledglings', from the root 'to sprout, to fly up'. Radak reads it as an image of young priests growing up beside the altar.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [are] the dwellers of your house; still they praise you. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy are those who live in your house. They are still praising you. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Having envied the birds, the speaker turns to the people who do live there: the priests, Levites and servants who sleep in the sanctuary precincts (Ibn Ezra, Radak). 'Blessed' (אַשְׁרֵי) is not a pious wish but an exclamation of congratulation: 'how fortunate!', the same word that opens the whole Psalter. The KJV renders עוֹד as 'still', which is right, but the sense is 'ever, continually': their praise never stops. The KJV prints 'Selah' as if it were a word of the poem; it is a musical or liturgical marker whose meaning is unknown. Treat it as a pause. A director should let the silence after 'praising you' hang, because the next verse widens the circle from residents to travellers.

philological_notes.note: 'How fortunate!' An exclamation of congratulation, not a prayer or a promise of reward.
Liturgical or musical marker of uncertain meaning; likely a pause or a lift.

verses.translation_literal: O the happinesses of [the] human whose strength [is] in you; highways [are] in their heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy the one whose strength is found in you. The highways are already laid in their hearts.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens a second 'happy' cry (the first was v. 5, 'happy are those who live in your house'), and the camera moves from those who stay to those who travel. The Hebrew is almost bare: 'strength for him is in you; highways in their heart.' Note the quiet slide from the singular 'human' to the plural 'their': one person, then the whole company. Ancient pilgrims depended on stamina and on God together; to an audience that walked uphill for days to Jerusalem, 'strength' (oz) is something you need in your legs, and the psalmist says it is located in God, not in the walker.

The key word is mesillot, 'highways': from the root for heaping up, so raised, built-up roads, not footpaths. The Hebrew has no 'to Zion'; the ASV and BBE add it, and the KJV's 'the ways of them' (with 'of them' in italics, supplied by the translators) is an attempt to make sense of a terse clause that blurs the image. The tradition splits on what is in the heart. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as the pilgrim road itself: they think in their hearts of the highways that go up to the house of the LORD, with no other desire or plan in mind. Radak, reporting his father's reading, takes the highways as paths of the knowledge of God held in the heart, which they walk back and forth daily. Rashi reads it as a person reckoning in his heart the ways of his own conduct, to straighten them. For an actor: the road is internal, and it is long before the feet move.

philological_notes.note: An exclamation of fortunate state, a plural construct from 'ésher', 'happiness'; it describes a condition, not a gift. It is a different word from 'blessed' (barukh, from the root ברך), which the KJV uses for both, hiding the repetition of ashrei at vv. 5, 6 and 13.
Raised, banked roads: built highways, not trails. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'a road and a path'. The Hebrew does not say where they lead; 'to Zion' in ASV and BBE is interpretation.

verses.translation_literal: Passing through the valley of the Baca, they make it a spring; also blessings the early rain covers [it].
verses.translation_dramatic: They walk through the Valley of Baca, and as they pass they turn it into a place of springs. The early rain wraps the valley in blessings.
verses.directors_commentary: The pilgrims are on the road. The Valley of Baca appears nowhere else: it may be a real dry valley on the pilgrim route, or a valley of baca shrubs (a thorny, balsam-like bush, as in 2 Sam 5:23–24), or, by a pun on בכה, 'to weep', a valley of weeping. The poet leaves all three alive; the KJV chooses a place name and loses the weeping, the YLT and ASV choose 'weeping' and lose the place. Hold the ambiguity. The pilgrims' passing makes a spring, as if their joy makes water flow in dry ground (Ibn Ezra reads it as the water that gathers where many feet go). The last clause hides a pun the KJV does not see: מוֹרֶה means both 'early rain', the first autumn rains that come after the dry summer (Joel 2:23, which is the right season for the autumn pilgrimage festival), and 'teacher, guide' (the YLT's 'director'), from the root 'to show, to instruct'. Rain and guide both 'cover' the valley with blessings. The KJV's 'filleth the pools' reads בְּרָכוֹת as בְּרֵכוֹת 'pools' (Radak notes the same) and so loses the word 'blessings' that the whole poem has been building. The verb עָטָה is 'to wrap, to put on as a cloak', a tender picture: rain as a garment.

philological_notes.note: Unique here as a valley name; elsewhere the plural bekha'im names a shrub or tree (2 Sam 5:23). A pun on 'weeping' (בכה) is probable.
Both 'early (autumn) rain' (cf. Joel 2:23) and 'teacher/guide' (from the root meaning 'to show, to teach'). Both senses fit the pilgrim road.
'To wrap, to cover as with a garment': the blessing as clothing.

verses.translation_literal: They go from strength to strength; he appears to God in Zion.
verses.translation_dramatic: They go on from strength to strength, until each one stands in Zion before God.
verses.directors_commentary: The road is long but the pilgrims grow stronger, not weaker: the opposite of what a hard journey does. 'Strength' (חַיִל) is also the word for an army or a company, so Radak and Metzudat David hear it as 'from one band to the next', the roads filling with groups of pilgrims joining into one great host; and Rashi hears it as study-house to synagogue. Hold both: stamina and company. The KJV 'every one of them' is an added gloss for a singular verb: the Hebrew says 'he appears', one by one, though the subject was a crowd. The verb is niphal, יֵרָאֶה, which in this setting is the standard phrase for 'appearing before God' at the festivals (Exod 23:17), and a careful reading sees a pun: the same consonants can be read 'he sees God'. The goal is 'Zion', named only now, at the end of the sentence, as the one word that turns the whole journey into arrival.

philological_notes.note: 'Strength' or 'army, company'. Two senses both work: growing in strength, and passing from one group of travellers to the next.
Niphal: 'he appears, is seen', or (read otherwise) 'he sees'. The standard idiom of festival pilgrimage.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, God of Jacob. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, God of hosts, hear my prayer. Turn your ear to me, God of Jacob. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn of the psalm. Since v. 2 the poet has already been speaking to God ('your dwellings', 'your altars', 'your house'), but only in exclamation and description: how lovely, how happy are those who. Here, for the first time, come imperatives: 'hear', 'give ear'. The voice drops from admiring a place to asking for something, and the singular 'my prayer' narrows the choir of pilgrims to one speaker. Play it as a held breath after a long song.

The Hebrew piles up three titles, YHWH, Elohim, Tseva'ot, 'YHWH, God of hosts', which the KJV compresses to 'O Lord God of hosts'; the heaped name is the language of a petitioner approaching a king. Ibn Ezra takes 'hosts' as the angels, matched by 'Jacob', whose sons are God's hosts on earth. The two verbs for listening form a pair: 'hear' (shama) and 'give ear' (ha'azinah), the second built from the noun 'ear' (ozen), literally 'ear it', 'bend your ear'. Rashi supplies what the prayer is for: that God build his house; Radak, to hasten the redemption. 'God of Jacob' ties the request to the ancestor who met God at a place he named Bethel, and Radak notes Jacob is the father of the tribes, a stranger to none of them. 'Selah' is a liturgical mark of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or lifting; Malbim takes it as 'end of the matter'. The KJV's 'Selah' simply transliterates it.

philological_notes.note: A verb made from the noun 'ear' (ozen): to 'ear' someone, to bend the ear toward them. Paired with shim'ah ('hear') it makes the petition a two-step: be told, then attend.
A marker of uncertain meaning in the Psalms, probably a pause or musical or liturgical lift; Malbim takes it as marking the end of the topic.

verses.translation_literal: Our shield, see, God, and look at the face of your anointed.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look, O God, our shield. Look on the face of the one you anointed.
verses.directors_commentary: The prayer becomes specific: it asks God to look at the king. 'Anointed' (מָשִׁיחַ) is the Hebrew word that became 'Messiah', but here it simply means the reigning king of the line of David, anointed with oil at his accession; the KJV's 'thine anointed' is accurate and carries the later weight without saying so. 'Face' is the subject of looking: to look at the face is to show favour (compare Num 6:25), so the request is that God smile on his king. 'Our shield' is either a title for God ('O God, our shield') or for the king, who is the people's protector (Ibn Ezra cites Ps 89:19, 'the Lord is our shield'); the syntax permits both and some, like Meiri, read it as an object ('see our shield'). The KJV 'Behold' is archaic for the plain imperative 'see'. Notice that both imperatives are the mirror of the eyes the speaker has been training on the sanctuary: now he asks God to look back.

philological_notes.note: 'Our shield'. A title for God (as in v. 12), or for the king as the people's protector; the syntax allows either.
'Your anointed one': the Davidic king, anointed with oil. Not yet the later technical sense of the end-time Messiah.

verses.translation_literal: For good [is] a day in your courts, more than a thousand; I have chosen to stand at the threshold in the house of my God, more than dwelling in the tents of wickedness.
verses.translation_dramatic: One day in your courts is better than a thousand anywhere else. I would choose to stand at the threshold of my God's house rather than live at ease in the tents of the wicked.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse that everyone remembers, and the KJV gets it half right. The first line is a plain comparison (a day is better than a thousand), and the Hebrew leaves open 'a thousand what': days, as the parallel suggests, or perhaps 'a thousand days elsewhere' (Metzudat David, Targum). The second line is where the KJV adds. 'Doorkeeper' (KJV, ASV) turns הִסְתּוֹפֵף into a job; the Hebrew is a rare verb built from סַף, 'threshold', and means to stand or loiter at the threshold: the lowest position, the beggar's place, outside the door. Rashi sees a man staying at the doorpost to keep watch; Radak sees a man staying in the entrance rather than owning a whole house abroad. 'Chosen' is a deliberate decision, not a resignation. And the contrast is with 'the tents of wickedness': 'tents' (אֹהֶל) are the home of the nomad and the foreigner, and 'dwelling' is the verb of settled, comfortable living. A threshold in a temple, a tent in the world: the speaker prefers the humblest place in God's house to the comfort of a rich household that ignores him. Radak and Meiri hear 'tents of wickedness' as the lands of the Gentiles. The word 'wickedness' (רֶשַׁע) is not neutral crime but a state of being out of order with God. Play the line as a decision, quietly made, not a boast.

philological_notes.note: A rare form (hithpael of the root of 'threshold'): 'to stand at the threshold'. Not 'to be a doorkeeper' as in the KJV.
'Tents of wickedness': the dwellings of the wicked, or (Radak, Meiri) the lands of the nations.

verses.translation_literal: For a sun and a shield [is] YHWH God; favour and honour YHWH gives; he does not withhold good from those who walk in blamelessness.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD God is a sun and a shield. The LORD gives favour and honour. He holds back nothing good from those who walk without blame.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem ends on two images and a promise. 'Sun and shield' pairs the thing that gives light and warmth with the thing that keeps off harm. Ibn Ezra notes that the pilgrim needs both: shelter from the sun of the road, and the sun's light. Here the KJV 'sun' is correct but its context is easy to miss: in the ancient Near East the sun was a god (Shamash in Mesopotamia, Re in Egypt), and to call YHWH 'a sun' while remaining within monotheism claims for him the role the nations give to a deity of light and justice; he is not the sun, but he does what the sun-god is said to do. 'A sun' is literally 'a sun', not 'the sun'. 'Favour' (חֵן) is the grace that makes someone welcome, and 'honour' (כָּבוֹד) is weight, status. 'Walk in blamelessness' (תָּמִים) means wholeness, with nothing missing, not sinlessness, and the verb 'walk' brings back the roads of verse 6. The KJV's 'no good thing will he withhold' is true to the Hebrew, though 'will' turns a general truth into a future promise; the Hebrew verb is a timeless imperfect. Echo the opening: the poem began with a longing and ends with a certainty. Rashi records a minority view in Midrash Tehillim that שמש here means 'battlement' (cf. Isa 54:12), a defensive wall: a nice fit with 'shield', but the plain sense is the sun.

philological_notes.note: 'Sun'. Also a divine name in the surrounding cultures (Shamash). Rashi cites a midrashic reading as 'battlement'.
'Whole, complete, blameless'. The sense is integrity rather than sinlessness.
'Favour, grace': the quality that makes a person welcome. Malbim notes that God gives both free grace and honour, which a human patron would not.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH of hosts, O the happinesses of [the] human trusting in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD of hosts, happy is the one who trusts in you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends where it keeps coming back to: ashrei, 'O the happinesses of'. This is the third such cry (vv. 5, 6, 13), and the last closes the circle: v. 6 said 'strength for him is in you' (bakh), and v. 13 says 'trusting in you' (bakh). Strength, then trust: the same 'in you' bracketing the whole pilgrimage. The first cry belonged to those who sit in the house, the second to those on the road; the last belongs to anyone at all, 'a human' (adam), with no pilgrim, priest or Israelite named. After the threshold, sun and shield of v. 12, a reader hears it as the answer to the petition of v. 9.

The KJV, ASV and Webster say 'blessed', which suggests a pronouncement of blessing (barukh). The Hebrew word is a cry of fortune, the plural 'happinesses', as YLT and BBE have it. The verse is also short on its own: Ibn Ezra links it to v. 12, reading it as the summary of that verse: whoever trusts in the Name will not lack good. Radak reads it as trust that does not despair during the long exile, trust in the day God brings the people out and rebuilds his house. Meiri hears a declaration: to show that he himself trusts, the psalmist says 'YHWH of hosts, happy is the one who trusts in you.' Play it quietly, as a settled thing and not a cheer.

philological_notes.note: 'O the happinesses of': an exclamation, plural construct of 'ésher'. Not the word for blessing (berakhah, H1293) and not the same as 'barukh', so 'blessed' in the KJV is a looser translation.
A present participle, 'one who trusts', the ongoing action of trust, not a single act; the rhyme with v. 6 ('in you') makes it the end of the strength-and-trust arc.
